passage.title: What Is Justice?
paras: We use the word 'justice' all the time: 'That's not fair!' is one of the first things children learn to say. But what does justice really mean?

At its simplest, justice means giving people what they are due. Someone who does wrong should face a fair consequence; someone who is wronged should be put right. A just society treats people fairly whoever they are: rich or poor, popular or not.

Justice is not the same as revenge. Revenge is personal and angry; it wants the other person to suffer, often more than they deserve. Justice is calm and fair. It follows rules that everyone knows in advance, it listens to both sides, and the punishment fits the wrong.

That is why courts have judges who must be neutral, and why everyone accused of a crime is 'innocent until proven guilty'. These ideas, called the rule of law, protect us all, because tomorrow it could be any of us standing in front of the judge.
Justice also looks forward. A fair system tries to help people change, so that the wrong is not repeated. A punishment that only causes pain, and teaches nothing, may not be just at all.

Many traditions place justice at the heart of a good society. In Islam, Allah commands justice and good conduct (Qur'an 16:90), and believers are told to stand firm for justice even against themselves (Qur'an 4:135).
So justice is essential: without it, the strong do as they please and the weak have nowhere to turn.
